t: Minimum Runes to Add — Counting Crystal-less Components
o: Restated plainly: after possibly adding new directed runes, every focus point must either hold a crystal or be reachable by magic flowing out of some crystal. The key observation comes from the examples: in Example 2, nodes 0,1,2 already have incoming edges, yet they still need help because no crystal can reach them — the cycle 0→1→2→0 is sealed off from the crystals at 3 and 5. Adding one edge 4→2 lets magic from crystal 3 flow into that whole cycle. So the real requirement is *reachability from a crystal*, not merely an incoming edge. Since one well-placed edge from any crystal-bearing region can feed an entire connected region of non-crystal nodes, the answer equals the number of weakly connected components (ignoring edge direction) that contain no crystal. With n up to 1e5 and m up to 2e5, we need a linear-time connectivity algorithm such as DSU or BFS/DFS.
k: The condition 'receives magic flow' means being reachable from some crystal through existing plus added runes — an incoming edge alone is not enough (see Example 2's crystal-free cycle).
One added rune from any crystal-containing node into a crystal-free component makes every node of that component reachable from a crystal.
Therefore the answer is exactly the number of weakly connected components containing zero crystals; direction of edges never matters for counting them.

a.i: Build the undirected version of the graph and run BFS/DFS from every unvisited node to enumerate weakly connected components. For each component, track whether it contains a crystal using a boolean array. Every component found without a crystal contributes exactly one rune to the answer, since a single edge from any crystal node reaches all of its members.
s: Build an undirected adjacency list from flowFrom/flowTo and mark crystal nodes in a boolean array.
Iterate over all nodes; when an unvisited node is found, start a BFS/DFS collecting its component.
During traversal, record whether any visited node holds a crystal.
If the finished component contains no crystal, increment the answer.
a.t: O(n + m) — building the adjacency list and visiting each node/edge once dominates.
a.sp: O(n + m) — adjacency list, visited/crystal arrays, and traversal stack.

a.i: Since only weak connectivity matters, DSU gives a compact linear solution: union the endpoints of every rune, then union nothing else. A component's root tracks whether it contains a crystal. Finally, count distinct roots whose flag is false — each needs exactly one added rune.
s: Initialize parent array and a hasCrystal flag per root, set true for crystal nodes.
Union flowFrom[i] with flowTo[i] for every rune, merging crystal flags.
For each node, find its root; collect roots whose merged flag is false in a set (or mark on first sight).
The size of that set is the answer.
a.t: O((n + m) α(n)) — near-linear union-find operations with path compression.
a.sp: O(n) — parent array and crystal flags (no adjacency list needed).

w: In an interview, lead with the reachability insight (Example 2 is the perfect probe — naive 'indegree ≥ 1' reasoning fails there), then present the BFS/DFS solution and mention DSU as a leaner alternative. Common pitfalls: (1) treating 'receives flow' as mere indegree instead of reachability from a crystal; (2) forgetting edge direction is irrelevant for counting components; (3) assuming a crystal-free component might need more than one rune — one edge suffices since the whole component becomes reachable. Edge cases: multiple crystals in one component, isolated non-crystal nodes, and crystals guaranteed non-empty so the answer is always achievable. Likely follow-ups: what if crystals could be empty (answer would be n or impossible depending on interpretation), or if added runes had costs (minimum-cost arborescence-style variant).
